meta: Sybrand van Beest's 1631 panel of the Russian embassy walking to the States-General in The Hague.
about: A procession of men in red velvet robes and plumed hats walks past a stone arcade toward the Binnenhof in The Hague. The Russian embassy reached Holland in the autumn of 1631. Officials brought the ambassadors from Texel through Muiden and along the Vecht, and the party included eight nobles, six officers, two priests, forty footmen and cooks. On 4 November they asked the States-General for an audience, and this panel shows them on the way. Sybrand van Beest painted it. The Rijksmuseum bought it from a dealer in 1895 after a Delft sale, where it was still listed as anonymous.

meta: Charles James Richardson's 1860 design for a library in Gothic Revival style, drawn in watercolor and ink.
about: Bookshelves rise to the ceiling in this library, and a carved stone fireplace stands flanked by statues. The ceiling is covered in intertwining arches, and the French doors are shaped as pointed arches with a cross above them and an overdoor molding of broken arches. A chimney and mirror sit at right center between large sculptures on plinths. The bookcases end in egg and dart molding. The museum calls the room a prime example of Gothic Revival vocabulary. Charles James Richardson drew it in 1860.

meta: Edmond Collignon's 1856 Allegory of Comedy, an overdoor panel from a Paris town hall wedding room.
about: A woman crowned with laurel rests her arm on a stack of books and holds a red comic mask high. She wears a white and gold drapery, and a dusky landscape of trees and a river opens behind her. Edmond Collignon painted this Allegory of Comedy in 1856 as an overdoor, a panel set above a doorway. It came from the decoration of the wedding room in the old town hall of the 8th arrondissement at 14 place des Vosges, now in the 4th. It is in the Musée Carnavalet in Paris.

meta: Edwin Willard Deming's 1890 painting The Mourning Brave, a man praying over a dead woman in a dim tent.
about: Light streams from above into a shadowed tepee, where a Native American man covers his face with his hands and prays over the body of a woman. Edwin Willard Deming painted it in 1890. In the story he gave it, the man asks the Great Mystery, shown as the light, to protect her spirit and guide it onward. The museum says Deming's paintings romanticized Native American lives and fed the myth of a vanishing race.

meta: Francisco Pacheco's Saint Agnes of Rome, one panel of a Seville altarpiece contracted in 1605.
about: Saint Agnes stands in a jeweled crown and halo, holding a palm frond in one hand and a white lamb in the other. Her embroidered silver gown has an orange skirt and a crimson mantle. Behind her lies a sparse landscape with bare trees. Francisco Pacheco painted the panel for the altarpiece of doña Francisca de León in the convent church of Santo Ángel in Seville, a commission he contracted in 1605. Dean López Cepero bought it in 1804 and ceded it to the Prado in 1829.

meta: Jusepe Leonardo's 1635 portrait of Alaric II, the Gothic king who died in battle in 507.
about: A bearded king in a gold crown, green armour and a flowing red cape holds a round shield, and a helmet and staff lie at his feet. Behind him a battle unfolds with mounted and foot soldiers under a cloudy sky. Jusepe Leonardo painted Alaric II in 1635. The Prado's notes say he succeeded his father as king of the Visigoths and died in the battle fought in 507 against the Frankish king. That defeat ended the Visigothic hold on Gaul, apart from Narbonne.

meta: A pair of late 1500s Kano Mitsunobu screens of birds and flowers that run from early spring to late autumn.
about: Across the pair of screens, the seasons run from right to left, beginning with a blossoming plum and ending with late autumn peonies. Three swimming ducks sit at the centre between early summer irises and early autumn bellflowers. At the right, birds of prey terrorize a pheasant and an egret, while a peacock and peahen converse at the left. The museum reads the hawks as signs of military strength and the peafowl as cultural prestige. The inscriptions are not signatures but an attribution to Kano Eitoku, written by his youngest brother Kano Naganobu.

meta: Polidoro da Lanciano's Madonna and Child with Saints Mark and Peter, painted around 1535.
about: Held by his mother, the infant Christ instructs Saint Mark, who sits on a lion, and blesses him with his right hand. Saint Peter stands near, recognizable by his keys. The Walters says the way the figures interact adds liveliness to an otherwise static grouping of the Virgin with two saints. It also notes that the idyllic landscape is characteristic of Venetian painting. Polidoro took his name from his native town of Lanciano, since in the Renaissance a last name was often only the city of a person's origin.

meta: Johann Georg Schwartze's 1850 portrait of Pieter Arnold Diederichs, the Amsterdam bookseller who founded a daily newspaper.
about: Pieter Arnold Diederichs sits almost full length in a long fur-lined coat, holding a copy of the Algemeen Handelsblad in his right hand. A small table and a bookcase stand at the right. He was an Amsterdam bookseller who founded the paper in 1828 and published it until his death. Johann Georg Schwartze painted him in 1850. The portrait came to the Rijksmuseum through the V.E.L. Diederichs-Portman Bequest.

meta: Charles S. Raleigh's 1870 painting of the schooner yacht America under full sail.
about: Heeled over and cutting through choppy dark water, the two-masted schooner America carries a full spread of white sails, with an American flag at the stern and a small red tender at the right. The original yacht was built in 1851 to enter the Hundred Guinea Cup, the only American entry against fourteen British vessels. The museum tells a story that Queen Victoria asked who was second, and the answer was that there is no second. The race later became known as the America's Cup. Charles S. Raleigh painted this view in 1870.

meta: Ole Peter Hansen Balling's Grant and His Generals, a group of Union officers painted from sketches made in the field.
about: Mounted officers in dark uniforms ride across a dusty field under the stars and stripes, and several riders in front are painted as individual portraits. Ole Peter Hansen Balling, a Norwegian artist, drew Abraham Lincoln at the White House in the autumn of 1864 and then got permission to paint leading Union generals from life. He joined Grant at City Point during the campaign against Richmond and spent five weeks sketching officers. Sheridan was painted in the Shenandoah Valley, while Sherman and Thomas sat for him in Washington after the war. The Custer portrait, second from the left, is thought to be the only one painted from life.

meta: Peeter Neeffs the Elder's 1636 painting of a Gothic church interior by candlelight.
about: Candlelight falls on the pointed arches and tall columns of a Gothic church, seen down the nave toward the east. Two boys with torches stand at the left. A mass is being held in a chapel at the right. Memorial boards hang on two of the pillars, one of them dated 1625, and a few visitors in period dress cross the black and white checkered floor. Peeter Neeffs signed the painting on a near pier and dated it 1636.

meta: Xu Daoning's hanging scroll Autumn river in the rain and clouds, an imagined riverscape of mist, fishermen and a lone scholar.
about: Mist and cloud hide the upper slopes of the mountains and give this imagined river valley a wet, autumnal mood. At the right a fisherman huddles in his small boat among the reeds. A path on the far shore leads from a hamlet to a stone bridge, and a wood gatherer comes down a narrow trail with two bundles of sticks on his shoulder pole. From a riverside pavilion a lone scholar looks out over the water. Opposite him a narrow waterfall drops through a series of cascades. The museum describes the inhabitants as a mix of peasants and scholar-recluses.
